title: Handling Events
summary: **Event handling** in React lets you respond to user actions — clicks, typing, form submits — by attaching functions to JSX props like onClick, onChange, and onSubmit, wrapped in React's cross-browser SyntheticEvent.

subtopics.title: Attaching handlers in JSX
subtopics.explanation: Add a function to an event prop such as `onClick`. React calls it when the visitor clicks. It is like connecting a doorbell button to the chime it should trigger.

subtopics.title: SyntheticEvent
subtopics.explanation: React gives your handler an event object with details about what happened. It provides a consistent way to read the click or key press across browsers. Think of it as a standard incident report.

subtopics.title: Event delegation
subtopics.explanation: Browsers can handle many child events through a shared parent listener. React uses delegation internally for many events. It is like one receptionist directing many visitors instead of putting a guard at every door.

subtopics.title: preventDefault
subtopics.explanation: `preventDefault()` stops the browser's usual action for an event. For example, a form handler can stop a page reload while it saves data. It is like pausing the default route to take a different one.

subtopics.title: stopPropagation
subtopics.explanation: `stopPropagation()` stops an event from continuing to parent elements. Use it only when a parent should not react to that event. It is like asking a message not to travel farther up the chain.

subtopics.title: Passing arguments to handlers
subtopics.explanation: Use a small function when a handler needs extra information. For example, `onClick={() => removeItem(id)}` passes the item's id after the click. It is like writing the recipient on an instruction before sending it.

subtopics.title: Capture vs bubble phase
subtopics.explanation: An event can travel from the outer page toward the target, then back outward. The capture phase happens on the way in; bubbling happens on the way out. It is like a visitor passing a lobby before reaching a room.

subtopics.title: Event pooling history
subtopics.explanation: Older React versions reused event objects, so developers had to copy event details before using them later. Modern React no longer pools events on the web. This is like an old rule that newer equipment made unnecessary.

foundations.overview: An event is something a visitor does, such as clicking or typing. React lets a component respond with a function called a handler. Think of a doorbell: the click is the ring, and the handler is what you do next.
foundations.formalDefinition: An event handler in React is a function passed to a camelCased event prop (onClick, onChange, onSubmit, etc.) on a JSX element. React invokes the handler with a SyntheticEvent — a normalized wrapper around the native browser event — when the corresponding DOM event fires.
foundations.whyItMatters: Events are the bridge between the user and your application state. Without event handlers a UI is static; with them you can update state, submit forms, and drive every interaction. Interviewers test events because almost every component you ever write will handle at least one.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of an event prop as a doorbell button. You hand React a function (the action to run when the bell rings). When the user presses the button, React rings the bell by calling your function and hands it a slip of paper (the event object) describing what happened.
foundations.browserPerspective: React does NOT attach a separate listener to every element. It attaches a few listeners at the root of your app and lets real DOM events bubble up to it — this is event delegation. When an event reaches the root, React figures out which component it targeted, wraps the native event in a SyntheticEvent, and calls the matching handlers in order.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Buttons that submit or save, text inputs that update state on every keystroke, forms that validate and submit, dropdowns that open on click, drag-and-drop, keyboard shortcuts — all of these are built on event handlers.
foundations.businessImpact: Smooth, correct event handling is what makes a product feel responsive. A button that does nothing, a form that reloads the page, or a double-submit that charges a card twice all erode trust and cost revenue.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Knowing how SyntheticEvents, delegation, preventDefault, and stopPropagation work prevents whole categories of bugs — accidental page reloads, events firing twice, handlers receiving the wrong arguments.
foundations.performanceImpact: Because React uses delegation, you rarely pay for thousands of individual listeners. The main cost to watch is creating a brand-new inline arrow function on every render, which can cause memoized children to re-render unnecessarily.
commonUseCases: Click handlers on buttons and links (onClick)
Reading input as the user types (onChange)
Passing extra arguments such as an item id to a shared handler
Stopping a click from bubbling to a parent (stopPropagation)

commonMisconceptions.myth: React attaches a real DOM listener to every element with an onClick.
commonMisconceptions.reality: React uses event delegation — it attaches a small number of listeners at the app root and dispatches events to your handlers from there.

commonMisconceptions.myth: The event object is a normal native browser event.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It is a SyntheticEvent — a cross-browser wrapper. Historically React pooled and reused these objects, so old code that read e.persist() did so to keep the event after the handler returned. Pooling was removed in React 17, so the event now behaves like a normal object.

config.intro: React doesn't listen on every node. Here is the path a real click takes from the browser to your function.

steps.name: User clicks
steps.detail: The browser fires a native click event on the target element (e.g., a <button>).

steps.name: Event bubbles
steps.detail: The native event bubbles up the real DOM tree toward the document/root where React listens.

steps.name: React catches it at the root
steps.detail: React's single delegated listener receives the event and identifies which React element was the target.

steps.name: SyntheticEvent is created
steps.detail: React wraps the native event in a normalized SyntheticEvent so behaviour is consistent across browsers.

steps.name: Handlers run in order
steps.detail: React calls your onClick handler (and any parent handlers as it walks up the component tree) with the SyntheticEvent.

steps.name: You control flow
steps.detail: Inside the handler you can call preventDefault() to stop default behaviour or stopPropagation() to stop bubbling to parents.

interactiveExamples.title: onClick, onChange, and onSubmit together
interactiveExamples.explanation: A button uses onClick, the input uses onChange to track typing, and the form uses onSubmit with preventDefault so the page does not reload.
interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: Typing updates state live; submitting shows a greeting without reloading the page; Clear resets both fields.

interactiveExamples.title: Passing arguments and stopping propagation
interactiveExamples.explanation: Each list item shares one handler but passes its own id via an arrow wrapper. Clicking Delete calls stopPropagation so it does not also trigger the row's select handler.
interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: Clicking a row selects it. Clicking Delete logs the id but does NOT select the row, because stopPropagation halts bubbling.

codeLab.title: Wire up a like button
codeLab.instructions: Add state for a like count and an onClick handler that increments it. Show the current count in the button label.
codeLab.expectedOutput: Clicking the button increases the like count shown in its label.
hints: Pass a function reference or arrow function to onClick, not a function call.
Use the functional updater setCount((c) => c + 1) so rapid clicks stay correct.

keyTakeaways: Event props are camelCased (onClick, onChange, onSubmit) and take a function reference, not a string or a function call.
React wraps native events in a cross-browser SyntheticEvent; event pooling existed before React 17 but was removed, so e.persist() is no longer needed.
React uses event delegation — a few listeners at the root, not one per element — which keeps large lists cheap.
Call e.preventDefault() to stop default behaviour (like form reloads) and e.stopPropagation() to stop bubbling to parent handlers.
To pass arguments, wrap the handler: onClick={() => handleClick(id)}; watch out for accidentally calling it during render.
